## Building Topshe: a voice assistant in the browser

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/topshe-browser-voice-ai

An experiment in browser-local language models, voice interaction and practical integration choices.

Topshe is a personal assistant experiment with language model inference in the browser. That is a specific technical boundary: it does not mean every speech feature is offline, every browser is supported, or every planned integration is already implemented. Start with a bounded experiment The product question is whether a small local model can make an assistant useful without routing every conversation through a hosted language model API. Topshe uses a quantised Qwen 2.5 model through wllama and WebAssembly, with a React interface and local conversation storage. The name comes from Feluda’s assistant in Satyajit Ray’s stories. In product terms, the intended role is similarly modest: help with a question or a small planning task. It remains an experiment, not a promise that a small browser model can replace a complete connected assistant. Local inference has a first use cost The documented model download is approximately 900 MB. That makes first use readiness a separate experience from later conversations. A progress state, recoverable downloads and an honest explanation of device requirements matter more than calling the product frictionless. Running inference locally also moves constraints onto the user’s device. Available memory, browser behavior and competing activity can affect the experience. There is no published representative device benchmark establishing a universal response time claim, so this case does not invent one. Separate the voice pipeline from the model The project uses browser speech APIs for recognition and synthesis. A browser can process speech differently from how the language model processes text. In particular, speech recognition may involve a remote service. A locally running model is therefore insufficient evidence for a claim that no data leaves the device. Wake word support uses Picovoice Porcupine and requires its own access key. Push to talk is a fallback. These are product dependencies, not details to hide behind a broad offline label. The MDN SpeechRecognition documentation https://developer.mozilla.org/en US/docs/Web/API/SpeechRecognition explains the browser support and remote processing caveats. Delivered scope versus future ambition The repository documents local conversation history with IndexedDB and an offline capable application shell. It also describes calendar, email, news and smart home integrations as planned. Those ideas should be read as a roadmap, not features a visitor can already rely on. WebGPU is not an established completed acceleration path in the documented implementation. Likewise, a compatibility statement in a README is not a substitute for a tested device matrix. Text only fallbacks and clear unavailable states are part of making the current scope understandable. The next useful evidence Before positioning this as a dependable assistant, I would want first use completion rates, model load failures, memory use and response latency across representative devices. Speech should be evaluated separately, with its permissions and processing path made visible. Integration tests should follow actual connected workflows as they are built. These are future validation needs, not results claimed from this project. The current artifact demonstrates browser local inference and the interface around it. The lesson is to make a narrow privacy claim accurately, and to treat dependencies and unsupported capabilities as part of the user experience. See the Topshe implementation and roadmap https://github.com/saswatasg/topshe for the documented architecture and current scope.

## TGB Hunt: orchestrating a self-hosted outreach workflow

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/tgb-hunt-linkedin-outreach-agent

Task orchestration, campaign state and lessons from building a self-hosted outreach experiment.

TGB Hunt is a self hosted Django and Playwright outreach experiment. Its useful engineering story is campaign tasks, state tracking and follow up orchestration. Its implementation can send automatically; it should not be described as a system where every message always receives human approval. The workflow behind the interface Outreach is a sequence of states rather than a single text generation task. A campaign needs to know what has been attempted, what remains pending, which connection requests have changed status and whether a follow up should be scheduled. Losing those distinctions can create duplicate or badly timed actions. The repository includes task handlers for connections, follow ups and pending request checks, alongside campaign records and background execution. Django provides the application and persistence layer; Playwright operates the browser. The language model participates in the workflow, but the product is not simply a prompt wrapped in a button. State is a product requirement A useful task record should distinguish intended work from attempted work and confirmed completion. Browser activity can fail in ways that are not equivalent: navigation may fail before an action, an action may complete before confirmation is recorded, or a platform state may change between checks. The project includes reconciliation and failed state handling. Those mechanisms are important implementation artifacts. They do not establish that every edge case is covered or that the platform will continue to accept the same interaction behavior. A reliable claim needs reproducible tests and operational evidence, not only the presence of task code. Correcting the approval claim The public connection task handler can perform the send action. The implementation reviewed here does not establish a mandatory human decision before each individual send. The earlier portfolio description of an always reviewed drafting agent overstated that boundary. A review first workflow would be a meaningful future product change: persist a proposed action, display its recipient and content, obtain approval, then execute and record the result. That is a recommendation, not an existing capability being claimed here. Platform constraints shape the product An external platform is more than a browser surface. Its policies, account permissions and interface changes constrain what a product can responsibly offer. LinkedIn documents restrictions around prohibited software and automated activity in its official help guidance https://www.linkedin.com/help/linkedin/answer/a1341387 . This project should therefore remain an archived technical experiment rather than a promise of dependable recruiter outreach. The portfolio does not claim policy compliance, zero account risk, universal compatibility or an unattended service guarantee. Those would require evidence beyond a working browser task. What is and is not measured The public record does not provide a traceable reply rate or meeting dataset. Repository history and release counts show development activity; they are not proof of user value or conversion improvement. A stronger future evaluation would measure task state correctness, duplicate prevention, recovery behavior and the distinction between drafted and executed actions. Any user outcome study would also need a defined sample, time window and attribution method. Until then, the defensible contribution is workflow engineering and an explicit account of its limitations. The TGB Hunt repository https://github.com/saswatasg/TGBhunt contains the implementation. It is presented here as an archive, with no invented business result.

## DhanPlan: monthly planning with visible assumptions

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/dhanplan-retirement-calculator

How DhanPlan connects Indian savings instruments, retirement withdrawals, gap-solving and stress scenarios in a versioned monthly model.

DhanPlan is an India focused retirement planning product. The current story is a monthly model connecting savings, assets and retirement withdrawals, with assumptions and limitations made visible. A projection is a scenario, not a guarantee or proof of financial model accuracy. A plan needs more than a final number A retirement target is useful only when someone can understand the path to it. Contributions occur over time, different instruments have different rules, assets may mature at different points and spending continues after retirement. A single compound growth figure cannot explain all of those interactions. DhanPlan’s product direction is to connect those elements in one plan. The interface needs to communicate which inputs drive the result and which changes are meaningful. Showing a large future corpus without explaining inflation or withdrawals would make the output easier to misread. Model the sequence month by month The published methodology for Engine 2.0.0 describes a monthly ledger with contributions, balances, instrument behavior and retirement withdrawals. The rules review date is 2 October 2026. Instruments include EPF, PPF, NPS, deposits, precious metals and property related cash flows alongside investment assumptions. The point of a shared ledger is consistency across the plan. A maturity event after retirement still matters; an asset should not silently disappear because it falls outside the contribution phase. Versioning also gives a correction a visible context instead of presenting every output as timeless truth. Make the gap actionable The gap solving feature reruns the model to explore the contribution change needed under the selected assumptions. It is different from promising that a particular investment will achieve the target. It depends on the same return, inflation, timing and cash flow choices as the underlying projection. Nominal and inflation adjusted views answer different questions. The former describes future currency amounts; the latter helps a person think about purchasing power. An understandable product keeps that distinction visible rather than switching between them without explanation. Stress the assumptions, not just the interface The documented stress scenarios include higher and lower assumptions and 1,000 Monte Carlo paths. These show how sensitive a plan can be to the selected inputs. Simulated paths are conditional on their modelling assumptions; they are not a complete picture of every possible future event. A helpful experience should let a user see which assumption changed and how the result moved. It should also explain when a feature is a deterministic calculation and when it is a simulated distribution. More scenarios are not automatically better if their meaning is hard to understand. Keep limitations beside the model The methodology documents limits around fees, exit costs, some tax timing and other instrument or household details. A calculator cannot infer every future household decision from a short form. The product should make exclusions discoverable and date sensitive rules traceable to the methodology. Financial accuracy, test coverage and adoption need their own independent validation. The delivered artifact is a live planning interface and a documented model; further verification should use reconciled fixtures and reproducible scenarios. The broader product lesson is to treat assumptions as part of the interface. A user should be able to inspect what a number means, change its inputs and understand where the model stops. See DhanPlan https://www.dhanplan.in/ and its current methodology https://www.dhanplan.in/methodology for the versioned rules and limitations.

## A data deep-dive that ends in a product decision

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/data-deep-dive-method

A practical method for connecting metric definitions, funnel evidence and user workflows to a testable product decision.

A useful data deep dive ends with a decision, not just a more elaborate dashboard. This article presents a reusable working method: define the question, check the measurement, inspect the journey, compare explanations and choose the next test. It is not a claim that every example was used in a particular client engagement. Write the decision before opening the dashboard Begin with the choice the team needs to make. Is a workflow failing, is a feature being bypassed, or is the measured population wrong? A question such as “why is conversion low?” is too broad until its entry event, completion event and qualifying users are defined. Decide what evidence would change the recommendation. This keeps a visually interesting chart from becoming the answer by default. Check the denominator and the event Before interpreting a decline, inspect whether the same action is counted consistently across devices and releases. Distinguish people, sessions, leads and transactions. Missing events, repeated submits and changes in consent can alter the apparent funnel. Keep an explicit note of the comparison period and known instrumentation gaps. A precise looking percentage can still describe the wrong thing. Connect the aggregate to a real journey A funnel identifies where the measured flow narrows. Session evidence and workflow conversations help explain what may be happening there. Neither is sufficient alone: a recording shows one experience, while an aggregate can conceal several different experiences. Google’s funnel exploration guide https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9327974 describes the measurement tool. The Clarity heatmap documentation https://learn.microsoft.com/en us/clarity/heatmaps/heatmaps overview describes behavioral views that can complement it. Compare explanations instead of collecting opinions Keep a short hypothesis list. For each explanation, record the supporting evidence, contradicting evidence, uncertainty and the cheapest useful next check. A validation problem, an unclear proposition and an existing external workflow need different responses. Prioritization should consider user impact and delivery constraints, not merely the number of people who favor an idea. A hypothesis is not a proven cause until an appropriate evaluation supports it. Leave the team with an actionable record The output should state the decision, scope, owner, success measure and unresolved questions. The LiveKeeping adoption investigation /case studies/livekeeping compliance gap shows workflow diagnosis in a specific setting; checkout work /case studies/cart checkout shows buying journey friction. Their reported numbers belong to their individual cases. Reusing the method does not imply that every new analysis will produce the same uplift.

## AI image greetings lifted feature engagement by 168%

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/ai-send-greetings-168

A dormant 'Send Greetings' feature, an image-gen model, and a festival calendar across 27 occasions — feature engagement up 168% at LiveKeeping.

At LiveKeeping, I worked on an AI image generation integration for the Pro+ Send Greetings feature and a geo segmented calendar of 27 occasions across five regional groupings. The supplied record reports +168% feature engagement; it does not establish the same increase in overall product retention or revenue. Give the feature a relevant moment The feature helps a merchant create greetings for customers. Its product challenge is broader than generating an attractive image: the occasion, language and business context need to make the greeting useful at the moment someone wants to send it. The documented work combines image generation with a regional festival calendar. This gives the product a structured source of relevant occasions rather than treating every user as if they follow the same national calendar. Five groupings provide a practical segmentation basis; they are not a claim to represent every local custom. Make the integration understandable The supplied work describes the Nano Banana image model integration and its role in producing greeting artwork. The product flow brings together the selected occasion, business context and image generation. A user needs to understand what will be created and have a clear path to review the result. An AI integration should be assessed through the task it helps complete. Generation availability alone does not show that someone created a usable card or sent it successfully. Those steps deserve separate instrumentation rather than one undifferentiated AI use counter. Calendar design is part of the product The 27 occasion calendar makes timing and relevance explicit. Regional mapping connects the schedule to the merchant’s context. The feature work also fits the broader lifecycle messaging architecture, where priority, daily limits and conflicting messages need to be considered. A useful notification is a prompt for a relevant task. Sending more reminders is not automatically better, and the calendar should not be interpreted as permission to contact every merchant for every occasion. The design needs a path from relevance to action, alongside controls for message fatigue. What the reported result means The supplied record reports a 168% improvement in feature engagement. The public evidence does not provide the underlying event definition, denominator, cohort dates or attribution method. This case therefore keeps the label at feature engagement, rather than presenting it as an increase in DAU, revenue, retention or cards per user. The reported engagement result describes the work record. A reproducible evaluation would define the eligible cohort, usage event and comparison dates before attributing a change to the feature. What I would measure next The next evidence pack should define the engaged action and comparison period, then separate generation attempts, successful images, user edits and completed sends. Regional uptake and repeat use would help distinguish one time curiosity from recurring usefulness. These are measurement questions, not results claimed here. The delivered story is a feature integration and a structured occasion calendar, with a reported engagement outcome whose measurement scope remains limited in the public case. Read the Send Greetings case /case studies/livekeeping send greetings alongside the notification architecture /blog/push notification architecture . Google's Gemini image generation documentation https://ai.google.dev/gemini api/docs/image generation provides the model context; it does not validate this product's engagement result.

## The 17:1 e-way bill gap: diagnosing B2B adoption

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/e-invoice-adoption-gap

A workflow investigation at LiveKeeping identified 17:1 and 19:1 adoption gaps and informed executive product discussions.

At LiveKeeping, investigating native compliance feature usage revealed a 17:1 E Way Bill gap and a 19:1 E Invoice gap relative to external Tally origin workflows. The work informed executive roadmap discussions. It does not establish a shipped connector or measured recovery in adoption. Ask where the work already happens A feature can be available to a paying customer without becoming their preferred workflow. For an accounting product, the surrounding system matters: invoices, bookkeeping and compliance activities are connected. Looking only at the native feature funnel can miss the substitute workflow a customer already uses. My work combined analysis of API transactions, product usage and workflow context. The purpose was to understand why users with access to native modules were still generating compliance documents elsewhere. This is a product discovery problem before it is a feature redesign problem. Keep the ratios tied to their scope The supplied work record reports a 17:1 E Way Bill gap and a 19:1 E Invoice gap, comparing external and native activity. These ratios describe the investigated usage context; they are not a market wide share estimate or proof that seventeen times as many distinct customers rejected the product. The underlying cohort table, time window and denominator are not reproduced publicly here. That limits how far a reader should generalize the result. A stronger evidence pack would show the qualifying subscriber cohort, event definitions, comparison period and treatment of repeated transactions. Translate the finding into a decision The analysis was presented at VP and CEO level and contributed to the roadmap discussion. The important change was the framing: low feature usage needed to be understood alongside the workflow customers were already completing outside the native interface. A connector, data transfer change or revised entry point could be options to investigate. This case does not assert that a particular middleware implementation was built, installed by 50,000 merchants or achieved a latency target. Implementation and rollout outcomes need separate evidence. Separate adoption from reliability A parallel workstream analysed 100K+ API transaction logs and addressed compliance journey errors. The supplied record reports a 58% reduction in rejection rate for that reliability work. This is a different measure from adoption: fewer rejected submissions do not establish that users moved their workflow into the native module. Keeping those results separate makes the case more useful. One stream asks why customers use another path; the other asks what fails when a compliance transaction is attempted. They may influence the same roadmap, but their outcomes should not be added together or treated as evidence of the same intervention. What the public case establishes The defensible contribution is analysis, problem framing and an executive narrative connecting feature usage to real workflows. It also shows the importance of distinguishing a diagnostic finding from a delivered solution. Further rollout claims would require release records, cohort adoption data and a measurement window. For the product context, see the official E Way Bill portal https://ewaybillgst.gov.in/ and the full compliance discovery case /case studies/livekeeping compliance gap . The lesson is to measure the work customers are completing, not simply the interface they are declining to use.

## Daily reporting: three sources, one dependable view

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/daily-report-automation

A LiveKeeping reporting workflow using Google Apps Script, 88 mapped rows and three data sources, with freshness and reconciliation made explicit.

At LiveKeeping, I built a Google Apps Script reporting workflow bringing Kibana, MongoDB and GA4 information into an 88 row daily report. The documented operating schedule was 11 AM. The useful product artifact is a repeatable reporting structure, with a defined mapping scope and daily operating expectation. Define what each row means Combining systems is not the same as making their figures comparable. A report needs a definition for each row: its source, qualifying population, time period and calculation. Subscriber counts, transaction activity and analytics events describe different objects. A single spreadsheet can make those differences easier to see or accidentally hide them. The mapping work is therefore part of the product decision, not merely preparation for the script. Separate collection from interpretation The pipeline consolidates information so the team can inspect it in one working view. That does not mean the system can decide why a metric moved. The report needs stable labels and enough context to support comparison; the analyst still needs to investigate a change. No production credentials, private database extracts or confidential records are reproduced in this article. Treat the schedule as an operating expectation The 11 AM report time describes the intended daily routine. Google Apps Script time driven triggers can run within a scheduled window rather than guaranteeing an exact second. A robust report should show when each source was last refreshed and whether the current run completed. See Google’s installable trigger documentation https://developers.google.com/apps script/guides/triggers/installable for scheduling behavior and account constraints. Build trust through reconciliation Useful validation compares a sample of mapped rows with their original sources, distinguishes missing values from zero and makes failed collection visible. Repeat runs should not silently duplicate figures or overwrite a valid prior result with incomplete data. Those are acceptance criteria for dependable reporting; this public case does not publish a full set of operational logs proving every condition. It also does not claim an independently verified number of hours saved. The next useful evidence To strengthen this case further, I would add an anonymized row dictionary, reconciliation fixtures and a run history example showing partial source failure. That would make reliability inspectable without exposing business data. The current contribution is the consolidated reporting workflow and its defined mapping scope. See the full reporting case /case studies/livekeeping report automation .

## Discovery that continues into solution delivery

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/discovery-to-roadmap

Building discovery at Upcore Technologies: structured research, opportunity prioritization and end-to-end solution delivery ownership for 23+ clients.

At Upcore Technologies, I built the discovery practice and derived solutions while managing their delivery end to end for 23+ clients. Structured conversations, a 500+ response survey and an evidence framework supported prioritization. The work connects problem understanding to solution definition and delivery ownership. Enterprise interest in AI is broad. A useful product direction needs a more concrete starting point: a workflow, a constraint and a reason to change it. Discovery helps define that starting point. Delivery tests whether the proposed solution can become something the client can use. What I worked on I built the discovery practice from scratch, including structured client conversations, a survey with 500+ respondents and a framework for organizing evidence into priorities. The work also included 20+ prospective client conversations across 12 verticals and a top three opportunity brief. Those counts describe research scope. They are not a combined sample, and the brief is a prioritization output rather than evidence that three products launched. Alongside discovery, I derived solutions and managed their delivery end to end for 23+ clients. I coordinated sprint planning and backlogs with a six developer team, without formal reporting authority. What the evidence needs to explain An interview count is useful context, but it does not explain a product decision by itself. A decision needs the problem, the evidence supporting it, the alternatives and the constraints. The following is a practical checklist for reviewing an opportunity brief—not a reproduction of a particular interview script or a confidential client artifact: Problem: Which workflow is difficult, and for whom? Evidence: What was observed directly, and what remains an assumption? Value: What changes if the problem is solved? Feasibility: What data, integration or operational constraints matter? Next step: What should be investigated, demonstrated or delivered next? The distinction between evidence and assumption matters throughout the process. A stated interest is different from budget approval. A positive demo reaction is different from production acceptance. A forecast is different from realized revenue. Carrying the solution into delivery Discovery and delivery belong in the same professional story because a proposed solution still needs definition and execution. My Upcore work includes both deriving solutions and managing their delivery for 23+ clients. Inventory Leveling & Procurement Intelligence /case studies/upcore inventory leveling is a public artifact within that work. The client demo connects orders, component requirements, stock and lead times to procurement planning. Its interface and calculation tests make the solution inspectable. The public repository and test documentation https://github.com/saswatasg/inventory leveling agent describe the implementation. It uses mock data and has no live ERP integration. That is its delivery stage, not a weakness to hide or a production outcome to invent. The artifact demonstrates a workflow and validated calculations; deployment and business impact require additional evidence. Measure the right kind of result For this work, three categories should remain distinct: Category What it establishes Research Scope, evidence and prioritization outputs Client delivery Responsibility for defining and carrying solutions through delivery Business impact Measured changes with a baseline, window and attribution A strong case study connects these categories where the evidence supports it. Its strongest evidence is the decision trail: what changed, why it changed and what the team delivered. Read the discovery and solution delivery overview /case studies/upcore discovery for the role and scope, or the qualification framework /case studies/upcore lead scoring for a separate example of turning information into an operational decision.

## Notification design: priority, relevance and restraint

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/push-notification-architecture

A lifecycle-messaging architecture for LiveKeeping: 27+ triggers, priority tiers, regional relevance and a three-slot daily cap.

At LiveKeeping, I redesigned the lifecycle messaging architecture around 27+ triggers, P0–P3 priority tiers, a three slot daily cap and five regional groupings. The deliverable is a messaging system and its operating rules; this note does not claim independently measured revenue recovery or a reduction in opt outs. Start with the reason for the message Renewals, transaction states, compliance errors and feature announcements serve different needs. A useful trigger inventory explains what changed, who needs to know and what action they can take. This makes it possible to distinguish an urgent operational message from a discretionary reminder before writing the copy. A catalogue of messages without this distinction is a list, not an architecture. Resolve conflicts before sending Priority only helps if the system has a rule for competing messages. The design uses P0–P3 tiers and a daily cap to make that decision explicit. The operational specification also needs to explain suppression, expiry and exceptions: a message can lose relevance while waiting in a queue. The public case documents the approach, but does not provide a complete production implementation that a reader should assume is reproduced here. Make the message relevant to the context The regional calendar brings occasion specific context into the same architecture as renewals and transactional messages. A calendar should support relevance rather than create an obligation to contact every user on every date. Plan eligibility and geographic context need to be applied before delivery. The greeting integration is a related feature, whose reported engagement result should remain distinct from the notification system itself. A measurement plan for the whole channel A sensible evaluation would track eligible users, suppression reasons, delivery, the intended action and disengagement. Opens alone do not show usefulness, and a declining complaint count can be misleading if delivery also fell. Comparisons need a defined cohort and period. These are recommended measurement questions, not results reported from this project. The useful takeaway The product contribution is to make messaging decisions consistent and understandable across teams. Trigger inventory, priority, conflict rules and contextual eligibility belong in the same specification. Read the notification case /case studies/livekeeping notifications and the Send Greetings story /blog/ai send greetings 168 . The Firebase messaging documentation https://firebase.google.com/docs/cloud messaging provides delivery platform context; it does not establish this project’s outcomes.

## FilmRisk.AI: what a weak backtest changed

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/film-risk-engine

A film-risk experiment with temporal validation, weak baseline comparisons and explicit data limits. What the evaluation changed.

FilmRisk.AI explores whether public film data can support a pre release risk score. The published evaluation did not establish a useful predictive advantage. That finding changes how the project should be presented: as an evaluation experiment, rather than a successful greenlight decision engine. The product question A score is only useful if it improves the decision someone could make without it. For a film risk product, an attractive interface or a complicated model does not establish that improvement. The relevant question is whether the prediction adds reliable information before release, using inputs available at that time. The project combines a gradient boosted model with empirical Bayesian priors and a component based scoring approach. Its implementation is in TypeScript with a Next.js interface. Simulation can describe uncertainty under assumptions, but it cannot repair missing data or prove that a score is commercially useful. Data coverage is part of the result The repository documents 2,454 film records spanning 2001–2025. Only 729 have the financial information required for training. This is not a representative financial history of every film in the period. It is a subset shaped by which figures were publicly reported and could be assembled. That missingness creates a practical constraint: the product must not imply that a score describes the whole industry equally well. Dataset size, the training subset and the population a model can reasonably speak about are different things. Test on later films, not shuffled familiarity The published primary evaluation uses 14 rolling annual folds with 658 tested films. This temporal approach asks whether knowledge from earlier releases helps with later releases. It is more relevant to a pre release decision than simply demonstrating a fit to familiar records. Outcome derived concept features were removed from the evaluation to address leakage. User supplied pre release concept inputs in the product are not thereby validated by that historical test. The distinction matters because the implemented interface and the tested prediction path need not be identical. What the benchmark actually says The published results report 29.3% classification accuracy, compared with 63.7% for a band median baseline and 80.5% for an always flop baseline. Greenlight precision was 11.3%, against a base hit rate of 11.0%. Reported RMSE was 1.303, compared with 1.23 for the band median baseline. These metrics answer different questions; they should not be collapsed into a single success percentage. In particular, high accuracy from predicting a dominant class is not a useful recommendation system. Conversely, these results do not justify marketing the more complex model as superior. They are published repository results, not an independently reproduced evaluation in this portfolio audit. What I would require before expanding it The next work should improve provenance, establish a decision relevant baseline and test the exact inputs used before release. A larger interface or more model components should follow evidence of usefulness, rather than substitute for it. A small recent holdout also needs its sample size made visible. The portfolio value here is the willingness to expose an unfavorable result and change the claim. This remains a research experiment. It should not be used as a validated financial decision tool. The implementation, benchmark and limitations are available in the FilmRisk.AI repository https://github.com/saswatasg/FilmRisk.AI and its published benchmark results https://github.com/saswatasg/FilmRisk.AI/blob/main/src/generated/benchmark results.json .

## Category pages: help customers make the next choice

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/category-page-redesign-plus34

A Sierra Living Concepts category-page redesign using analytics and session evidence, with reported lead outcomes kept within their measurement scope.

At Sierra Living Concepts, I led category and landing page work informed by GA4 events, Clarity heatmaps and analysis of 1.1M BigQuery events. The supplied record describes a four week sprint and reports +34% qualified leads. This note explains the decision and its measurement boundaries rather than inventing a complete experiment log. A category page has a job to do A product grid is useful when the customer already knows how to choose. A considered furniture purchase can require more context: which options fit the need, what customization involves and why the next step is worth taking. The product question was how the category journey could support that choice. More content is not automatically more help; its position and relevance need to be tied to the customer’s decision. Bring behavior and event data together Event analysis helps locate the transition from category exploration to product detail or an enquiry. Heatmaps and recordings add evidence about what people encounter along that path. The data does not explain intent by itself, and a handful of sessions does not prove how the whole audience behaves. The useful work is to connect those perspectives into a clear problem statement and a prioritized change. Make the next step understandable The redesign replaced a commodity presentation with a more contextual, trust led journey. A stronger page helps a visitor understand the category, inspect relevant products and choose what to do next. This is a description of the product direction, not a claim that one particular layout suits every category. Google’s funnel exploration guide https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9327974 and Microsoft’s Clarity documentation https://learn.microsoft.com/en us/clarity/heatmaps/heatmaps overview provide the measurement tool context. Read the reported results carefully The supplied work record reports +17% session to product detail clicks, +34% qualified leads, −16% bounce and +27% add to cart. These measures describe different stages of the journey. They should not be added together, and a +34% qualified lead figure should not become a claim of +34% revenue. The public case does not reproduce raw cohort data, a randomization record or a complete attribution analysis. What would make the evidence stronger An anonymized event dictionary, comparison dates and a clear definition of a qualified lead would let a reader assess the result more precisely. It would also help distinguish this initiative from other product page work reporting an add to cart improvement. The defensible story is the analytics led redesign and its reported outcomes, with their scope kept explicit. See the category case /case studies/category discovery and the related lead form work /blog/lead form overhaul 124 .

## Lead routing: observed signals and explicit pilot targets

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/lead-routing-gold-silver-bronze

Designing a tiered lead-allocation system at Sierra Living Concepts, separating observed source performance from pilot targets.

At Sierra Living Concepts, I designed a Gold/Silver/Bronze lead allocation system using source performance, agent capacity and escalation rules. The observed conversion data informed the design. The target of 5.2 to 3.5 days to close is a pilot objective, not a demonstrated result. The decision behind the queue The work addressed how a four agent team should allocate leads arriving from six sources. Giving every source the same handling path ignores differences in intent and conversion. A useful routing system needs to translate those differences into a next action without making the source label permanent. The available analysis reports website form conversion at 63.5%, chat at 4.7% and cart abandonment leads at 0.4%. These are observed source rates in the analysed dataset. They do not establish a universal probability of closing the next individual lead, and low volume categories need particular care. Three tiers, different handling Gold prioritizes high intent sources for specialist attention. Silver provides a structured follow up path for intermediate intent. Bronze reduces repetitive manual handling while retaining a route to human review when stronger intent appears. The important product choice is to make the next action clear. A tier alone is not enough: the team needs assignment rules, capacity handling and escalation conditions. A response indicating a substantial custom order can justify reconsidering a low initial priority. This is operational decision logic, not a learned model being claimed to predict every outcome. Capacity changes the routing decision Availability and agent specialization matter alongside source performance. The allocation design considered day by day coverage and a specialist path for high intent enquiries. Those rules should be evaluated against both response delay and conversion; waiting for a specialist is not automatically better than a prompt response. Coverage and timing decisions should be evaluated against qualified lead outcomes. The source record does not establish an independent conversion advantage from delaying a particular day’s leads. The Salesforce guide to lead management https://www.salesforce.com/sales/lead management/ provides broader process context, not validation of this case's results. Targets are not outcomes The supplied case describes a 30 day pilot progressing toward rollout. The design included targets for routing accuracy, automation coverage, specialist lead allocation and reducing days to close from 5.2 to 3.5. A target remains a target until a comparable post change measurement is available. The earlier portfolio presented 90% routing accuracy, 90% chat automation and increased daily specialist leads as achieved results. This revision treats them as pilot objectives. It also removes a dollar saving estimate presented as if the money had been recovered. Expected conversion revenue is a scenario, not realized savings. The evidence that would close the loop A stronger follow up would report assignment compliance, response time, escalation errors and conversion by source and handler over a defined period. Lead quality and seasonal changes need to be accounted for when comparing before and after. The team also needs to know whether the system improved workload balance rather than only moving one metric. This case establishes an allocation design grounded in observed source differences, with an explicit measurement plan. It does not claim a causal increase in revenue or a verified reduction in days to close. See the full lead allocation case /case studies/sierra lead allocation for the routing and pilot structure.

## Lead forms: diagnose the field, improve the journey

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/lead-form-overhaul-124

A Sierra Living Concepts form redesign: field-level diagnosis, inline validation and category-specific modules, with reported results in context.

At Sierra Living Concepts, a field level investigation identified a restrictive phone format check contributing to abandonment. The redesign combined clearer input guidance, inline validation and category specific form modules. The project record reports +124% submissions in 28 days. Start with the interaction, not the form length An aggregate completion rate tells a team that people are leaving. It does not tell them which interaction needs attention. The useful question was where users hesitated or failed: field entry, validation, submission, or the next step. GA4 field level events and Microsoft Clarity session evidence helped connect the measured funnel with the experience of filling out the form. The project record attributes 23% of drop offs to a restrictive field. That finding supported a focused intervention rather than a blanket recommendation to remove fields. Make the expected action understandable The redesign addressed three connected needs: Change User need Visible format guidance Understand what the field accepts before an error Inline validation Recognize and correct a problem while entering information Context specific labels Understand why the information is needed Category specific modules made the form more relevant to the enquiry. A customer asking about custom furniture should encounter a form that supports that task. Faster initialization and mobile interaction details also mattered: a clear field cannot help if it appears unresponsive. Evaluate the complete journey The project record reports +124% submissions , −41% mobile completion time and −68% rage clicks . These outcomes describe different aspects of the experience. More submissions should also be evaluated against lead quality; faster completion should not depend on confusing defaults or skipped information. A separate role level record reports conversion moving from 2.14% to 4.40% , approximately +105% . The available records do not establish a shared denominator and comparison window. I keep these figures separate rather than present them as consecutive stages of the same experiment. For implementation guidance, web.dev’s form curriculum https://web.dev/learn/forms covers input behavior, validation and accessibility. What I would make inspectable next An anonymized field event dictionary, before and after screenshots and a qualified lead comparison would strengthen the public evidence. The reported results describe the work record; the raw event export is not reproduced here. For another form, I would begin with the same diagnostic discipline: define completion, inspect field errors, watch mobile interactions and choose a bounded change. Removing fields can be useful, but only when the evidence supports it. See the full lead form case /case studies/lead form and checkout investigation /blog/checkout abandonment 73 to 54 .

## One useful change at a time: a growth learning loop

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/one-fix-a-week-cro

A practical framework for choosing, shipping and evaluating focused growth improvements without turning activity into a success metric.

A focused growth loop makes a small product change inspectable: one hypothesis, a bounded intervention and an explicit evaluation. This is a practice framework drawn from the kind of work I do. It is not a promise of one successful experiment every week or a historical record of an exact weekly shipping cadence. Choose a decision sized problem Start with a specific point in the journey rather than a broad redesign brief. A field validation error, unclear next action or mismatch between an advertisement and its landing page can become a bounded hypothesis. The intervention should be small enough to explain. It also needs to matter: changing a decorative detail without evidence of user friction may produce activity without improving the product. Write the hypothesis and the guardrails A useful hypothesis names the affected users, the change and the expected behavior. Define the main outcome alongside a guardrail such as qualified lead quality, completion errors or support burden. A higher submission count can be a poor result if the team receives unusable enquiries. Capture the measurement window before launch so the evaluation does not move opportunistically toward whichever metric looks favorable. Match the evaluation to the available traffic A weekly planning rhythm does not guarantee that a result can be measured in seven days. The required duration depends on traffic, effect size, seasonality and the chosen design. Google’s funnel exploration documentation https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9327974 is useful for understanding the measured journey, but a funnel comparison alone does not establish causality. Distinguish an observed change from an experiment capable of attributing it. Keep a decision log, including failures Record what shipped, what changed, what stayed uncertain and whether the team retained or reversed the intervention. A null result can be useful if it narrows the explanation. A failed change should not disappear from the learning record. The purpose is to make the next decision better, rather than celebrate a growing count of releases. Fixes with an obvious correctness requirement also need not be forced into a conversion experiment. Use the loop without promising the outcome The checkout case /case studies/cart checkout , lead form work /case studies/lead form and category page case /case studies/category discovery show distinct initiatives. Their reported outcomes should not be summed into a universal weekly growth claim. The reusable discipline is narrower: identify friction, make a clear change and evaluate it at the right scope.

---

## Checkout friction: from one metric to specific fixes

URL: https://saswatasg.com/blog/checkout-abandonment-73-to-54

A Sierra Living Concepts checkout investigation across 480K sessions, with reported abandonment moving from 73.1% to 53.9%.

At Sierra Living Concepts, a checkout investigation across 480,000 sessions connected funnel data with session evidence. The reported abandonment rate moved from 73.1% to 53.9%: a 19.2 percentage point change, or approximately 26% relative reduction. One rate, several possible explanations A checkout abandonment rate does not explain the interaction that caused someone to leave. Cost clarity, validation and payment recovery can create friction at different points. Treating them as one undifferentiated problem makes it difficult to choose a useful change. My contribution was to connect the measured journey with the actual checkout experience, then translate the findings into targeted improvements with the team. The scope included 480,000 sessions , GA4 funnel instrumentation and Microsoft Clarity evidence. Diagnose the step before choosing the solution A useful investigation defines the entry event, completion event and population before interpreting a drop off. A cart visitor and someone who has begun checkout are different populations. Device segments matter too: a field can behave acceptably on desktop while creating friction on a small screen. The working approach combined step level measurement with session inspection. Analytics showed where the measured flow narrowed; session evidence helped identify plausible interaction problems. A recording explains an individual experience rather than proving that every abandoned session had the same cause. Google’s funnel exploration documentation https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9327974 explains how to define and inspect a measured journey. Make the next action easier to complete The work focused on clearer checkout interactions within the existing storefront. The relevant design concerns included cost visibility, validation feedback and payment error recovery. Each needs its own acceptance criteria: can a customer understand the amount, correct an input and continue after an error? This is also where product management connects diagnosis with delivery. A finding must become a bounded implementation decision, a shared requirement and a way to check whether the change behaves as intended on mobile. Keep the outcome and its limits clear Reported measure Result Abandonment 73.1% → 53.9% Relative abandonment reduction Approximately 26% Mobile conversion rate +47% Checkout completion +49% Analysis scope 480,000 sessions The supplied record reports these outcomes. The public article does not reproduce a randomized experiment, raw event export or full attribution model. The percentages describe different metrics and should not be summed, or converted into an unsupported revenue estimate. External cart abandonment benchmarks also use populations that may not match this checkout. The reusable lesson The useful habit is to move from a broad metric to a specific decision: define the journey, inspect the friction, agree a change and evaluate it against a stable definition. Preserve a guardrail for errors and customer confidence as well as conversion. See the full checkout case /case studies/cart checkout , the related lead form redesign /blog/lead form overhaul 124 and the data deep dive method /blog/data deep dive method .
